newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco tells traders to hold off on price hikes.
newsitem.headline: Morocco tells traders to hold off on price hikes.

text.p: Morocco, which is undertaking a gradual liberalisation of commodity markets, has ordered local traders to delay the rise of sugar and edible oil wholesale prices, traders said on Wednesday.
"The government has informed Morocco's edible oil and sugar associations to delay the expected price increase until further notice," a Casablanca-based leading trader said.
He said the government earlier set March 15, 1997 as date to begin the increase in edible oil and sugar products prices on the domestic market, the trader said.

"The commodity operators were expecting to increase the prices by up to 11 percent depending on products categories. But unfortunately the authorities changed their mind and delayed the commodity price adjustment," he added.
An official at the trade ministry said "at this stage nothing has been published in the Official Bulletin to confirm commodity wholesale price rise(s) this month."
There was "an agreement of principle" for sale price increases but under special conditions related to many factors including social issues, he added, but gave no other details.

The government subsidises imported edible oil and sugar at an average of 5,000 dirhams ($532) and 2,000 ($213) per tonne, respectively, the trade ministry said. It also maintains control over the sale prices to avoid shortages and speculation on the domestic market, the ministry added.

"Today, what we neeed is a freedom of movement in real time and possibility of adjusting prices to the market needs...It is business freedom...And what should be in this country," said Driss Amar, head of Morocco's edible oil producers told Reuters.

Last year, Morocco launched a four-year gradual commodity liberalisation programme, including cereals aimed at complying with the World Trade Organisation rules but local industry faced a tough competition from foreign businesses, a market analyst said.
"The government is obliged to slow the liberalisation rhythm to avoid a sudden social crisis," the analyst added.
Morocco imported more than 500,000 tonnes of raw sugar, nearly 50 percent of the country's annual consumption.
Domestic consumption for sugar and edible oil is expected to grow by an estimated 3.0 percent in 1997, officials said.
